verdicts.reason: A correction for selection induced by incomplete eligibility under a missing-at-random assumption addresses a real component of the problem. It does not identify true eligibility when absence conflates unmeasured ineligibility with lack of testing under missing not at random, so partial address is appropriately limited.

item.problem_title: An unrecorded eligibility criterion is indistinguishable from a criterion that was met
item.problem_statement: Trial eligibility is assessed at a screening visit; a database records what a clinician happened to order. Restricting an emulation to patients with complete eligibility information can bias it when observation of the criterion depends on determinants of treatment or outcome that the recorded history does not adequately control, which is the ordinary case when testing tracks severity and access. Weighting and missing-data methods for unrecorded eligibility now exist in more than one paper. The harder version remains: eligibility is latent rather than merely missing, since an absent creatinine value is consistent both with a patient who would have failed the criterion and with one who was never tested. item.paper: Adjusting for selection bias due to missing eligibility criteria in emulated target trials.
item.evidence: The framework is built precisely for the case where eligibility cannot be ascertained for everyone, and it names the two current practices, exclusion and carrying forward the most recent value, as unexamined sources of bias. It supplies a correction under a missing-at-random condition and quantifies the cost of ignoring the problem at up to 10 percent of the effect size.
item.quote: In practice, patients with incomplete eligibility data are frequently excluded from analysis6 despite the possibility of selection bias.

verdicts.reason: A correlation and relative odds ratio across selected TTE-RCT pairs describe concordance within that sample; they do not provide a transport or selection model for predicting performance on a new question or database. The quoted result contains no target performance estimand, overlap condition, or validation of extrapolation.

item.problem_title: There is no theory for extrapolating successful replication of selected trials to new questions
item.problem_statement: A successful replication calibrates one emulation of one trial in one database. Transferring that confidence to a different question, or to the same question in a different database, is not an inference the benchmarking design licenses: it requires a target performance estimand stated in advance, an explicit selection or transport model, conditional exchangeability across the questions being compared, and overlap in whatever modifies emulation quality. Outside that support the transfer is model-dependent rather than identified, and frameworks that have been proposed for it remain unevaluated in that role. The benchmarking corpus is also a selected sample: trials get emulated when they are recent, large and have an accessible active comparator, which are the conditions under which emulation works best. item.evidence: This puts a number on how far replication success transfers: a correlation of 0.55 across 82 pairs means agreement on any single new question is weak, and the three named impairing factors are properties of the emulation rather than of the method. The 0.86 for closer designs is a within-sample subgroup finding, so the higher figure describes pairs already judged well matched rather than predicting a new one.

verdicts.reason: Reporting a correlation, relative odds ratio, confidence intervals, and heterogeneity is materially more informative than a binary agreement label. These summaries do not align paired estimands or decompose estimand mismatch from sampling error, so they only partially address the stated problem.

item.problem_title: Replication is reported as a binary label rather than as a calibrated comparison of estimands
item.problem_statement: Agreement between an emulation and a trial is informative only when the estimands, populations and measurements are close enough to be comparable, and better design alignment is empirically associated with stronger concordance. The benchmarking programs report this in graded form. What is cited downstream is a binary label, usually derived from interval overlap or direction agreement, and that label discards magnitude and uncertainty and cannot diagnose why two estimates differ: two studies estimating the same quantity imprecisely agree by that criterion, and two estimating different quantities precisely disagree. No reported measure, graded or binary, separates estimand mismatch from random error, because doing so requires aligning the estimands first and then reporting a paired contrast with joint uncertainty, which no benchmarking report currently does as a matter of course.
item.paper: Concordance between randomized controlled trials and target trial emulation: A meta-analysis
item.evidence: Concordance is reported as a correlation and a relative odds ratio with heterogeneity rather than as a count of pairs that agreed, which is the calibrated comparison a binary label cannot give. The summary ratio of 0.99 conceals both the 0.55 correlation and the outcome-specific bias, showing that one aggregate agreement number is not enough on its own.

verdicts.reason: The decision not to proceed is a documented example of data fitness stopping an emulation rather than merely being asserted narratively. Because the decision was not governed by prespecified quantitative thresholds, it does not supply the general stop rule the problem identifies.

item.problem_title: Data-fitness assessment is narrative and has no thresholds that would stop a study
item.problem_statement: Electronic health records arise from encounters, billing and documentation rather than from scheduled research assessments, so eligibility and follow-up in an emulation partly reflect care-seeking and access rather than the biology the protocol intends. Whether a given database can support a given target trial is a question about the data source and the protocol jointly, and quantitative assessments of that pair now exist. What does not exist is a prespecified stop rule: a threshold agreed before the analysis, on observability, temporal precision, capture continuity, comparator support, outcome validity and linkage completeness, that would halt a study when an essential component fails. item.evidence: This is one of the rare documented cases where a data-fitness judgment actually stopped an analysis: the team could have proceeded by assuming all discontinuations were clinically valid, and instead declined. What it does not supply is any threshold: the stop rested on expert input and a targeted literature review, no completeness fraction or measurement standard was named in advance, and the decision is described as a judgment the team felt was less than ideal either way.

verdicts.reason: Prespecified, registered contingencies and blinding to results can prevent outcome-informed protocol revision from invalidating inference for the planned adaptive design. The framework does not provide general post-selection inference for protocols selected after examining outcome-relevant analysis data.

item.problem_title: Inference conditions on a fixed target trial that was in fact selected after seeing the data
item.problem_statement: Eligibility thresholds, comparators, grace periods, washout windows and outcome definitions are routinely revised after investigators inspect the data. When outcome-relevant information from the analysis data is used to select among candidate protocols, a confidence interval calibrated for a protocol fixed in advance need not have nominal coverage for the selected estimand, unless the selection is incorporated into the inference or separated out through independent data. Saying so requires naming the target of inference and whether the coverage claimed is conditional on the selection or marginal over it, and applied reports do neither. item.paper: Illustrating an Adaptive Prespecification Framework for Observational Research: Target Trial Emulations Comparing Immunomodulator Treatments for COVID-19.
item.evidence: This closes part of the entry by making the data-driven revision of the target trial itself auditable: contingencies 2.1 to 2.3 redefined treatments from class level to tocilizumab versus baricitinib and restricted eligibility, and they fired against thresholds fixed in a registered protocol before the data were touched, with postbaseline decisions taken while blinded to results. What remains open is that the final published inference is still reported conditional on the revised trial, the thresholds themselves were partly arbitrary, and no comparable rule tells a reader how much of the estimate movement to attribute to the revision.

verdicts.reason: Publishing the base case, permitted deviations, triggered changes, and an abandoned secondary emulation makes some rejected alternatives and decision paths visible. It is an exceptional reporting framework rather than a registration system that routinely preserves all alternatives and their timing.

item.problem_title: Registrations record the final protocol and not the alternatives that were rejected
item.problem_statement: An emulation makes many defensible decisions: active comparator, washout period, time zero, grace period, how treatment episodes are constructed, censoring rules, follow-up length and outcome definition. Each has more than one reasonable answer, and the set of answers is the researcher's degrees of freedom. Design guidance exists and states that the operational methods remain scenario dependent, so it narrows the set without closing it. Registrations record the specification that was finally run and not the alternatives considered, the order in which decisions were made, or which were revised after the data were inspected. A final protocol snapshot cannot reveal what was never logged, so a reader cannot distinguish a protocol written once from one converged upon, and no later audit can reconstruct it.
item.paper: Illustrating an Adaptive Prespecification Framework for Observational Research: Target Trial Emulations Comparing Immunomodulator Treatments for COVID-19.
item.evidence: The rejected alternatives are published here rather than discarded: the Base Case plan is reported alongside its successors, and a second emulation in critical COVID-19 is reported as abandoned because no permitted deviation satisfied the baseline diagnostics. The entry stays open because this required a bespoke protocol and a journal article to accomplish; the registry entry itself recorded only the plan, and the paper states that criteria for refining plans are not routinely documented in prespecified protocols.
item.quote: No combination of permitted deviations from the Base Case approach was sufficient in satisfying predetermined baseline diagnostic criteria for this secondary study objective.

verdicts.reason: The cited restrictions identify concrete treatment-history strata with structural nonpositivity and alter the target population accordingly. The report does not provide a prespecified policy-specific support criterion, a complete enumeration of unsupported histories, or a formal surviving estimand.

item.problem_title: Positivity diagnostics describe weights instead of naming which patient histories are unsupported
item.problem_statement: A deterministic treatment strategy can assign a treatment that clinicians almost never give to patients with certain covariate histories. The standard response is to inspect the weight distribution and truncate the tail. Truncation is bias-variance regularization: it cannot identify an effect where the treatment density is structurally zero, and a marginal weight summary does not say which intervention-relevant histories carry small or zero density. What a reader needs and does not get is a policy-specific support criterion fixed in advance, diagnostics localized by time and by history, the fraction of the target population that fails the criterion, and the estimand that survives once those strata are set aside. Empirically, poor overlap has been shown to defeat adjustment methods that were otherwise well specified, which is the failure a weight histogram is least able to show. Software

item.evidence: Two positivity failures are named as histories rather than as weight statistics: hospitalizations from June to November 2020, when Janus kinase inhibitors were not in use, and patients receiving inpatient dialysis, for whom Janus kinase inhibitor cautions apply in severe renal impairment. Both were removed by restriction, which is what the entry asks for. It stays open because the remaining diagnostics are weight descriptions, a maximum of 20.711 and truncation at 6 standard deviations, and because random positivity violations are noted without being enumerated.

verdicts.reason: The federated approach addresses aggregation under an explicit condition that sites differ in baseline covariates but share a treatment effect, and the comparison illustrates sensitivity to aggregation method. That assumption leaves unresolved whether sites operationalized eligibility, treatment, and outcomes as materially different trials, so partial address is appropriately narrow.

item.problem_title: Averaging site estimates in a federated emulation can conceal that the sites emulated different trials
item.problem_statement: Distributed health data improve power and support transportability, and patient-level sharing is often prohibited, which is why federated emulation has been developed to the point of pooled-equivalent estimation for time-to-event outcomes. The statistical machinery for combining site estimates is not the hard part. Sites differ in coding systems, treatment availability, confounding structure and time resolution, so one executable protocol can define materially different eligibility, exposure and outcome at each site, and pooling then averages several different questions. Aggregation cannot detect that: heterogeneity between site estimates is produced equally by real effect modification and by mapping failure. Local validation and aggregate diagnostics shared without patient records can flag some of it, and no current practice requires either, or requires the target population and pooling
item.paper: Federated target trial emulation using distributed observational data for treatment effect estimation.
item.evidence: The framework does close part of the entry: it demonstrates that averaging site estimates is not innocuous, since fixed and random effects meta-analysis of the same nine pantoprazole site estimates produced opposite directions, and it supplies a federated fit whose global covariate balance ratio of 0.926 exceeds the 0.767 of fixed effects meta-analysis. What it does not close is the case the entry names: heterogeneity is assumed to reside in baseline covariates and not in the treatment effect, and under that assumption sites emulating genuinely different trials remain indistinguishable from sites with different case mix.
